questions.stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a cough that has lasted more than 3 weeks. He also reports night sweats, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, decreased appetite, and low-grade fevers that spike in the evening. His sputum has recently become streaked with blood. He travels frequently on overseas mission trips. Examination shows mild lymphadenopathy and crackles over the upper lung fields. Chest radiography shows upper lobe infiltrates with slight cavitation and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Acid-fast staining of sputum shows pink, slightly bent, beaded rods. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Chronic cough with hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, upper lobe cavitary disease, and acid-fast bacilli in sputum is classic active tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis causes the vast majority of human mycobacterial infections and produces a slow, progressive illness with dyspnea, cough, and hemoptysis. Reactivation disease characteristically involves the upper lobes with cavitation and drains to hilar and mediastinal nodes. The organism appears as a slightly bent, beaded, acid-fast rod on Ziehl-Neelsen stain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M. avium is a Mycobacterium avium complex organism that causes severe disease almost exclusively in immunosuppressed patients, most often as lymphadenitis or disseminated infection rather than cavitary lung disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M. intracellulare is the other member of the Mycobacterium avium complex and, like M. avium, is rarely pathogenic in a person with a healthy immune system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. leprae is the mycobacterium that causes leprosy, not a chronic cavitary pulmonary infection with hemoptysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is not acid-fast and causes acute lobar pneumonia over days, not a multi-week wasting illness with cavitation.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Sputum from a 45-year-old woman with a 6-week productive cough is examined in the laboratory. A Gram stain of an adequate specimen shows no organisms. The laboratory notes that the suspected pathogen has a cell wall with a very high lipid content. Which of the following stains is most likely to demonstrate this organism?

explanation.summary: Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli demonstrated with the Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain, not with Gram stain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lipids and glycolipids of the mycobacterial cell wall prevent uptake of Gram stain, so microscopic visualization of sputum or other fluids requires a special stain. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain, also called the acid-fast stain, is used for this purpose. Mycobacteria stain pink and are therefore called acid-fast bacilli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Giemsa stain is not the special stain required to visualize the high-mycolic-acid cell wall of mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: India ink preparations demonstrate a polysaccharide capsule by negative staining and would not reveal a lipid-rich bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylene blue is used as a counterstain and for gram-negative organisms such as Neisseria; it will not highlight mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silver staining is used for organisms such as Pseudomonas and Helicobacter pylori, not for demonstrating acid-fast bacilli.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A microbiology resident notes that a bacillus recovered from a patient with chronic pneumonia cannot be visualized with Gram stain despite repeated attempts. Which of the following cell wall features best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high content of hydrophobic long-chain mycolic acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps crystal violet

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thick polysaccharide capsule external to the cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide endotoxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete absence of a cell wall in this organism

explanation.summary: Mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall prevent uptake of Gram stain, which is why these organisms require acid-fast staining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacteria are protected by a lipid-containing cell wall rich in mycolic acids, in contrast to typical bacteria whose cell walls have a high peptidoglycan content. These acids cannot take up Gram stain. This is the structural reason mycobacteria are identified as acid-fast bacilli rather than as gram-positive or gram-negative organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A thick peptidoglycan layer is the feature of gram-positive organisms, which retain crystal violet and stain readily; mycobacteria have relatively little peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A polysaccharide capsule does not block Gram staining of the underlying cell; encapsulated organisms are still visible on Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lipopolysaccharide-rich outer membrane is a gram-negative feature; such organisms still take up Gram stain and appear pink.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycobacteria do have a cell wall; it is its lipid composition, not its absence, that defeats Gram staining.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A physician suspects pulmonary tuberculosis and submits a sputum specimen for culture, making a special request of the laboratory. Growth of this organism requires a particular medium on which it forms large colonies with a waxy appearance. Which of the following media is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis requires special media, most commonly Lowenstein-Jensen medium, on which it forms large waxy colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacteria will not grow on routine culture media, so a specific laboratory request must be made when tuberculosis is suspected. Lowenstein-Jensen medium is the common medium used. Because the organism grows slowly, detection can take up to 10 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chocolate agar is a routine enriched medium used for fastidious organisms such as Neisseria and Haemophilus, not for mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MacConkey agar is selective for gram-negative enteric bacilli and does not support growth of mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blood agar is a general-purpose medium used for organisms such as Pseudomonas and streptococci; mycobacteria will not grow on it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thayer-Martin agar is a selective medium for pathogenic Neisseria species and has no role in mycobacterial culture.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A sputum smear from an immunosuppressed patient shows pink bacilli on acid-fast stain. The laboratory reports that this result alone cannot establish which mycobacterial species is present and recommends culture or polymerase chain reaction testing. Which of the following best explains this limitation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria also stain acid-fast and look identical

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal respiratory flora in sputum also retain the acid-fast dye strongly

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stain binds host inflammatory cells rather than bacterial cell walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stain cannot distinguish living organisms from organisms already killed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The stain detects organisms only when they are present in very large numbers

explanation.summary: Acid-fast staining is nonspecific among mycobacteria, so culture or PCR is needed to identify the species.
explanation.whyCorrect: The acid-fast stain will show pink bacilli whenever a mycobacterium is present, but some non-tuberculosis mycobacteria stain acid-fast as well. There is no reliable way to differentiate M. tuberculosis from other mycobacteria microscopically. In uncertain cases, a culture or PCR analysis is required for organism identification.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ordinary respiratory flora are not acid-fast, so they are not the source of the ambiguity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stain highlights the mycolic-acid-rich bacterial cell wall, which is exactly why mycobacteria appear pink.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Viability is not what is in question here; even a smear full of viable bacilli would not reveal the species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sensitivity at low organism burden is not the stated problem; the issue is that a positive smear does not identify which mycobacterium is present.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A public health officer investigates two clusters of mycobacterial lung disease. In the first cluster, caused by M. tuberculosis, every case could be traced to contact with another infected person. In the second cluster, caused by Mycobacterium avium complex, no person-to-person link could be established. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: M. tuberculosis is acquired by the fecal-oral route, while Mycobacterium avium complex is inhaled

choices.label: B
choices.text: M. tuberculosis lives only in the human respiratory tract, while MAC lives in the environment

choices.label: C
choices.text: M. tuberculosis survives in soil and water, while Mycobacterium avium complex is carried only by humans

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are not acid-fast and therefore cannot spread between people

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex requires an arthropod vector, while M. tuberculosis spreads in droplets

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis has no environmental reservoir and spreads person to person, whereas Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are environmental.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis is not found in the environment; its only reservoir is the human respiratory tract, where it lies dormant and is later spread by coughing if disease reactivates. Mycobacterium avium complex bacilli are common environmental organisms found in soil, water, and animals. Patients acquire them by inhaling bacilli from those sources rather than from another person.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M. tuberculosis is contracted by respiratory inhalation, not orally, so the fecal-oral route does not apply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two organisms: M. tuberculosis is the one restricted to humans, and Mycobacterium avium complex is the environmental group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are acid-fast; indeed, that is why an acid-fast smear cannot distinguish them from M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither organism requires an arthropod vector; Mycobacterium avium complex is acquired from contaminated soil, water, or animals.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A research laboratory grows a clinical isolate of M. tuberculosis and observes that the bacilli aggregate into long, serpentine ropelike bundles. The responsible cell wall component is also toxic to mammalian cells and inhibits neutrophil migration. Which of the following is this component?

explanation.summary: Cord factor is toxic to mammalian cells, inhibits neutrophil migration, and produces the characteristic long serpentine colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cord factor is one of the proposed virulence factors of M. tuberculosis. It damages mammalian cells directly and blocks neutrophils from migrating to the site of infection. It also causes the bacilli to grow in the long, cord-like serpentine arrangements from which it takes its name.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokine release and helps the organism resist host oxidative stress; it does not produce serpentine cords.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is an outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria and is not a mycobacterial virulence factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is present in small amounts in mycobacteria and is not responsible for cord formation or neutrophil inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Purified protein derivative is the antigen preparation injected for the tuberculin skin test, not a virulence factor.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Alveolar macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis generate reactive oxygen species in an attempt to kill the organism. One mycobacterial cell wall component both induces host cytokine production and allows the organism to withstand this oxidative stress. Which of the following is this component?

explanation.summary: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokines and enables M. tuberculosis to resist host oxidative stress.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipoarabinomannan is listed among the proposed virulence factors of M. tuberculosis. It stimulates the release of host cytokines and confers resistance to the oxidative killing mechanisms of the macrophage. This contributes to the organism's ability to persist inside the phagocyte that ingested it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cord factor is toxic to mammalian cells and inhibits neutrophil migration; resistance to oxidative stress is not its described role.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycolic acid confers natural antibiotic resistance and immune evasion through extreme hydrophobicity rather than by defeating oxidative stress.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is an antibacterial compound produced by the activated macrophage to kill the bacilli, not a mycobacterial product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teichoic acid is a gram-positive cell wall constituent and is not part of the mycobacterial cell wall.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: An isolate of M. tuberculosis is found to be intrinsically resistant to many traditional antibiotics and also evades the host immune response. Both properties are attributed to extremely hydrophobic long-chain fatty acids in its cell wall. Which of the following components is being described?

explanation.summary: Mycolic acids are long-chain, extremely hydrophobic fatty acids that convey natural antibiotic resistance and help mycobacteria evade the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycolic acid is the defining structural feature of the mycobacterial cell wall. Its high content makes the bacillus tough and resistant to damage, conveys natural antibiotic resistance, and helps the organism evade host immunity. It also slows growth, which is why mycobacterial infections tend to be chronic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A polysaccharide capsule is not described as a mycobacterial virulence factor in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cord factor is defined by its toxicity to mammalian cells and inhibition of neutrophil migration, not by conveying broad antibiotic resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokines and resists oxidative stress; it is not the component that confers natural antibiotic resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptidoglycan is the major wall constituent of typical bacteria, and mycobacteria are distinguished by having relatively little of it.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: After inhalation, M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but continues to replicate inside them. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this intracellular survival?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism escapes from the phagosome and replicates freely in the cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism lyses the macrophage within minutes of being ingested by it

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism replicates only outside cells, within the alveolar lining fluid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism secretes a capsule that prevents opsonization by complement proteins

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bacillus lives within phagosomes of alveolar macrophages. Normally phagosomes fuse with lysosomes, which supply the enzymes needed to kill the organism. M. tuberculosis prevents this fusion by blocking macrophage intracellular calcium and acidification, so the bacilli grow within the phagocyte rather than being destroyed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The organism remains within phagosomes rather than escaping into the cytoplasm; that is where its growth occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rapid lysis of the macrophage is not the mechanism of early survival; the bacilli first grow quietly within intact macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary infection is characterized by macrophage invasion and intracellular growth, not extracellular replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The bacterial surface is in fact coated with C3b, which promotes rather than prevents recognition by complement receptors.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient's M. tuberculosis isolate is reported by the laboratory as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Resistance to which of the following is required for this designation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fluoroquinolone and another second-line drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isoniazid and a second-line injectable agent

explanation.summary: MDR-TB is defined by resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotic resistance is one of the virulence properties of M. tuberculosis. When an isolate is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin, the disease is referred to as multidrug-resistant TB. Such resistance limits treatment options, extends treatment time, and increases cost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus another second-line drug is what is added on top of MDR-TB to make an isolate extensively drug-resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolone resistance belongs to the definition of extensively drug-resistant TB, not to the definition of MDR-TB.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Resistance to a second-line injectable agent is part of extensively drug-resistant disease rather than the MDR-TB definition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance to a fluoroquinolone is a feature of extensively drug-resistant disease, and rifampicin resistance alone does not define MDR-TB.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: An isolate of M. tuberculosis that is already resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin is additionally found to be resistant to a fluoroquinolone and to at least one other second-line drug. How is this isolate best classified?

explanation.summary: Extensively drug-resistant TB is MDR-TB that is additionally resistant to a fluoroquinolone and at least one other second-line agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDR-TB denotes resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone and at least one further second-line drug. Each step up in resistance further limits treatment options, lengthens therapy, and raises the cost of care substantially.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atypical mycobacteria refers to the Mycobacterium avium complex organisms, not to a resistant M. tuberculosis isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The isolate is resistant to at least four agents, so it is by definition not drug-susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent infection describes an asymptomatic walled-off infection, a clinical state, not a drug-resistance pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multidrug-resistant disease stops at resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin; this isolate has additional second-line resistance.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with 4 days of fever to 104.5 F, nonproductive cough, headache, and watery diarrhea. He stayed at a hotel one week ago, and two other guests from the same hotel have been admitted with pneumonia. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. Chest radiograph shows a dense lower lobe consolidation, and a urine antigen test is positive. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Hotel or cooling-tower exposure with high fever, diarrhea, hyponatremia, a lobar pattern, and a positive urine antigen points to Legionella pneumophila.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is acquired from contaminated water aerosols such as hotel cooling towers, and outbreaks cluster among people at one site. Fever above 104 F occurs in about 20% of patients, watery diarrhea in 25-50%, and hyponatremia (sodium below 131) is a recognized clinical clue. Unlike the other atypicals, Legionnaires' disease commonly shows a lobar pattern on imaging, and the urine antigen test is the rapid confirmatory test described for this organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes mild atypical pneumonia with diffuse patchy opacities and is diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification, not urine antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds and is not transmitted by contaminated water systems.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. pneumoniae causes gradual, mild walking pneumonia with interstitial infiltrates and is not detected by a urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia but is not linked to cooling-tower outbreaks, diarrhea, or hyponatremia in this brick.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has had a dry, hacking cough, low-grade fever, malaise, and headache for 3 weeks. Several students on his dormitory floor have had similar illnesses. He looks well and walks into clinic unassisted, but chest radiograph shows streaky, patchy interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than his symptoms suggest. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Mild, gradual-onset 'walking pneumonia' in a young adult with dormitory clustering and radiographic findings out of proportion to symptoms is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired and atypical pneumonia in children and young adults, and outbreaks occur in college dorms, military barracks, and daycares. It is often called walking pneumonia because the illness is mild and self-limiting. Lung involvement frequently appears more severe than the patient's symptoms suggest, with streaky or patchy interstitial infiltrates on imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Legionnaires' disease typically affects patients over 40 and presents with high fever and a lobar pattern, not a mild 3-week course in a well-appearing student.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is listed as a cause of severe pneumonia in ICU patients, not mild ambulatory illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes rapid-onset illness with a productive cough and lobar consolidation.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pet-store employee who recently began caring for newly arrived macaws and cockatoos develops 10 days of fever, fatigue, sore throat, and a dry cough. Chest radiograph shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Atypical pneumonia in a person with occupational bird exposure is psittacosis, caused by Chlamydia psittaci.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. psittaci is named for its association with psittacine birds such as parrots, cockatoos, and macaws. It is not transmitted person to person; infection follows contact with infected birds, so cases occur in people who work around birds or keep them as pets. Its clinical picture is otherwise indistinguishable from C. pneumoniae, ranging from flu-like illness to severe pneumonia with high fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae presents identically but spreads person to person by respiratory droplets, with no bird link.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. influenzae is a typical pathogen causing productive cough and is not bird associated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L. pneumophila comes from contaminated water aerosols and usually causes higher fever with a lobar pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. pneumoniae spreads person to person and has no zoonotic reservoir described here.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought in with fever and a rash that began on his face and spread to his trunk. Over the past day he has developed painful erosions of the lips and oral mucosa, and examination shows target-like lesions with skin detachment over about 10% of the body surface. He had a respiratory illness with a dry cough 2 weeks ago and takes no medications. Which of the following organisms most likely triggered his condition?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most frequently identified infectious trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially in children and adolescents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and its more severe form, toxic epidermal necrolysis, involve painful rashes and blisters of skin and mucous membranes at sites such as the lips, nose, eyes, and genitals. The mechanism is an immune-mediated response triggered by certain infections and medications that causes cell death and detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes. Although medications are the most common cause overall, among infections M. pneumoniae is the one most often identified, particularly in this age group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia but is not identified as a common trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci can disseminate to liver, heart, and brain, but is not the typical trigger of this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila causes severe pneumonia with gastrointestinal symptoms, not this mucocutaneous syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a typical pneumonia pathogen and is not linked to this syndrome here.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with 2 weeks of gradual-onset malaise and a dry cough is treated with high-dose amoxicillin for presumed pneumonia. She shows no improvement after several days, and sputum culture on routine media grows nothing. Which of the following features of the responsible organism best explains the failure of therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alternates between elementary and reticulate bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion inside macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no cell wall for the drug to act on

choices.label: D
choices.text: It hides within a large cytoplasmic inclusion body

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes an enzyme that destroys the drug

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall, so antibiotics that inhibit cell wall synthesis are inherently ineffective.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is the tiniest free-living organism capable of self-replication and lacks a cell wall entirely, which also makes it pleomorphic. Because beta-lactams work by inhibiting cell wall synthesis, they have no target in this organism. Atypical pneumonia is in fact defined as pneumonia caused by non-classical pathogens that do not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The elementary and reticulate body cycle belongs to Chlamydia species, not Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion is how Legionella survives in macrophages and does not explain beta-lactam failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth inside a large inclusion body is a Chlamydia feature, not a Mycoplasma feature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-lactamase production is not described as the mechanism of resistance for this organism.

questions.stem: A respiratory isolate from a young adult with atypical pneumonia will grow only on media supplemented with cholesterol, and after prolonged incubation the colonies have a characteristic fried-egg appearance. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae requires sterols in its culture medium and forms fried-egg colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sterols are present in the M. pneumoniae cell membrane, a feature rare among bacteria, and culturing the organism therefore requires that sterols be present in the media. In culture the colonies take on a fried-egg appearance, and the memory hook offered is that eggs contain cholesterol, linking the colony shape to the growth requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae is an obligate intracellular organism that requires cell culture rather than enriched agar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci likewise grows only inside living host cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila needs iron and cysteine on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, not sterols.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae grows readily on standard laboratory media without added sterols.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 35-year-old is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and will be treated as an outpatient. Besides Streptococcus pneumoniae and respiratory viruses, which of the following groups of organisms are among the most common causes of pneumonia in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Legionella species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella species, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella species, and gram-negative bacilli

explanation.summary: Outpatient community-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and respiratory viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microbial causes of community-acquired pneumonia differ by site of care. In outpatients, the listed organisms are S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, C. pneumoniae, and respiratory viruses. Legionella species appear among hospitalized non-ICU and ICU patients, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli appear in the ICU group, reflecting more severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. trachomatis causes urethritis and eye infections rather than community-acquired pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative bacilli and S. aureus are ICU-associated, and C. psittaci requires bird exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella is a hospitalized-patient pathogen here, and C. trachomatis is not a pneumonia pathogen in this list.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are the organisms listed for ICU patients with severe pneumonia, not ambulatory patients.

questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae must first attach to ciliated epithelial cells of the lower airway before it can enter cells and establish infection. Which of the following mediates this attachment?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flagella and pili on the bacterial surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surface proteins of the elementary body

explanation.summary: P1 is the virulence factor by which M. pneumoniae binds ciliated respiratory epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae attaches to respiratory epithelial cells using the virulence factor P1, which binds ciliated epithelial cells in the lungs and facilitates entry of the bacteria into cells. After attachment there is roughly a 2 to 3 week incubation period before the gradual onset of symptoms, which is why the illness is easy to miss early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A capsule is not among the virulence factors described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagella and pili are how L. pneumophila attaches to respiratory epithelium and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. pneumoniae has no cell wall and is not described as using an O antigen for adherence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elementary bodies are the infectious form of Chlamydia species, not a Mycoplasma structure.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man shares a dormitory room with a student who has just been diagnosed with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. If he becomes infected, approximately how long after exposure would symptoms be expected to begin?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has a roughly 2 to 3 week incubation period followed by gradual onset of symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: After P1-mediated attachment to ciliated epithelium, there is approximately a 2 to 3 week incubation period before symptoms begin gradually. This long incubation and insidious onset contrast with the 2 to 10 day incubation and rapid progression seen with Legionnaires' disease, and they help explain why outbreaks in closed settings unfold slowly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to two days is far shorter than the incubation described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Months-long latency is not described for M. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Four to six days approximates the Legionella range, which is 2 to 10 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incubation of hours would suggest a toxin-mediated illness, not Mycoplasma infection.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 10-day history of dry cough, low-grade fever, and headache, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is suspected. Which of the following tests provides the most accurate and rapid confirmation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinin titer on chilled serum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: PCR performed on a respiratory specimen

explanation.summary: PCR is the most accurate and rapid way to diagnose Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: None of the clinical manifestations of M. pneumoniae infection are distinct enough to separate it from other atypical pneumonias, and the organism grows only on specialized Eaton agar over weeks. As with viruses, PCR can be performed on patient samples, and it is explicitly the most accurate and rapid way to establish the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold agglutination is nonspecific and is no longer recommended now that better tests exist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar is the medium for Legionella, and Mycoplasma requires sterol-containing media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism has no cell wall and is not seen on Gram stain of sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urine antigen test described in this brick detects Legionella, not Mycoplasma.

questions.stem: A resident proposes mixing a patient's serum with red blood cells and chilling the mixture to support a presumptive diagnosis of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Which of the following is the best reason this test is no longer recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be performed once antibiotics are started

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects only a single serotype of the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is nonspecific; other conditions cause agglutination

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires living host cells to propagate the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires several weeks of incubation to be read

explanation.summary: Cold agglutination testing has been abandoned because it is not specific and better tests are now available.
explanation.whyCorrect: Historically, cold agglutination tests supported a diagnosis of M. pneumoniae: patient serum was mixed with red blood cells and chilled, and antibodies caused the cells to clump. Combined with the clinical picture it served as a quick presumptive test, but it is not specific because other conditions also cause cold agglutination. Since more specific tests such as PCR are now available, cold agglutination is no longer recommended.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prior antibiotic use is not the stated limitation of this test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Detection of only one serotype describes the Legionella urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Requiring living host cells describes Chlamydia culture, not a serum agglutination assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weeks of incubation describes Eaton agar culture, not the agglutination test, which is quick.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old with patchy interstitial infiltrates has sputum and blood cultures that show no growth after 48 hours, and the team concludes the illness must be viral. Which of the following best explains the negative cultures if Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It circulates only in blood and never in the airway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It grows only within living host cells and cannot be cultured

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is destroyed by the transport medium used for sputum

choices.label: D
choices.text: It needs iron and cysteine that standard media lack

choices.label: E
choices.text: It needs specialized Eaton agar and weeks of incubation

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes culture-negative pneumonia because it requires specialized Eaton agar and weeks of growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae can be cultured only on specialized Eaton agar, which is not typically stocked in clinical laboratories, and the culture takes weeks. As a result the organism produces culture-negative pneumonia, which makes a virus appear to be the cause and contributes to the infection being underdiagnosed. Rapid PCR testing is what resolves the picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The organism infects the respiratory tract and is transmitted by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Obligate intracellular growth requiring cell culture describes Chlamydia species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction by transport medium is not the explanation given for negative cultures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron and cysteine requirements belong to the fastidious Legionella pneumophila.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who hikes weekly in wooded areas of the northeastern United States develops a slowly expanding red rash on his thigh 10 days after a camping trip. He is diagnosed with Lyme disease. The bite of which of the following arthropods most likely transmitted this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amblyomma americanum, the lone star tick

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dermacentor andersoni, the Rocky Mountain wood tick

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dermacentor variabilis, the American dog tick

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged or deer tick

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick

explanation.summary: Lyme disease is transmitted by the bite of the blacklegged (deer) tick, Ixodes scapularis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in mice and is transmitted to humans by Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged or deer tick. Lyme disease occurs most frequently in the northeastern United States, matching this patient's exposure. Ixodes scapularis is also a vector for Ehrlichia species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lone star tick transmits Ehrlichia species and is associated with alpha-gal syndrome, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Rocky Mountain wood tick is one of the ticks that carries Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The American dog tick is a Rocky Mountain spotted fever vector and is the species most often implicated in that disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brown dog tick transmits Rickettsia rickettsii; it is not a vector for Borrelia burgdorferi.

questions.stem: A public health officer is explaining how Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in nature before ticks transmit it to humans. Which of the following serves as the reservoir for this organism?

explanation.summary: Mice are the reservoir for Borrelia burgdorferi; ticks acquire the organism from them and pass it to humans.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reservoir of Borrelia burgdorferi is mice. Ixodes ticks feed on infected mice and subsequently transmit the spirochete to humans during a prolonged blood meal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cattle are not the reservoir for this spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dogs can be bitten by ticks but are not the reservoir that maintains Borrelia burgdorferi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Humans are incidental, dead-end hosts and do not maintain the organism in nature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deer support the tick life cycle but are not the reservoir named for the spirochete itself.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman finds a tick attached to her calf after gardening and removes it within 2 hours. She asks about her risk of acquiring Lyme disease. Which of the following best explains why her risk is low?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the larval stage of the tick is able to transmit the organism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only ticks that have fed on deer rather than mice carry the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tick must feed for 36 to 48 hours before transmission

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transmission occurs only in autumn, when adult ticks are feeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transmission occurs only when the tick is crushed during removal

explanation.summary: Lyme transmission requires roughly 36 to 48 hours of tick attachment, so prompt removal rarely results in disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: For Lyme disease to occur, the tick must be attached for 36 to 48 hours. Removing the tick promptly after the bite rarely results in disease, which is why tick checks after outdoor exposure are effective prevention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nymph is the stage usually responsible for transmission, and adults can transmit as well.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mice are the reservoir; the risk relationship described here is not what determines transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nymphs typically feed in the spring and summer, when most transmission occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission depends on duration of attachment, not on whether the tick is crushed.

questions.stem: Most patients who acquire Lyme disease never notice the tick that bit them, and most transmission occurs in the spring and summer. Which stage of Ixodes scapularis is usually responsible for transmitting the infection?

explanation.summary: The immature nymph is the usual culprit in Lyme transmission because it is small enough to go unnoticed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The nymph form of Ixodes scapularis is the usual culprit because nymphs are very small and easily go unnoticed, allowing them to stay attached long enough to transmit the spirochete. Nymphs typically feed in the spring and summer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult females can transmit the organism, but their larger size means they are usually seen and removed first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adult males, like adult females, are large enough to be noticed and removed before transmission occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eggs do not feed on hosts and cannot transmit infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The larva is not identified as the usual transmitting stage for human Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man develops a red, slowly expanding rash with a target-like appearance on his flank 12 days after a tick bite. Which of the following skin findings is pathognomonic for Lyme disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bullous lesions scattered over the trunk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maculopapular rash beginning on the wrists

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicular rash confined to one dermatome

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans, the expanding bull's-eye rash, is pathognomonic for Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema migrans is a red, expanding rash that gradually enlarges and can take on a bull's-eye appearance. It is pathognomonic for Lyme disease and, when present, allows a clinical diagnosis before serology becomes positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bullous lesions are not a common presentation of Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A maculopapular rash starting on the wrists and ankles is the pattern seen in Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A petechial rash is more characteristic of Rocky Mountain spotted fever as its vasculitis progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A dermatomal vesicular rash is not among the rashes described for Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A physician counsels a patient that the absence of the characteristic Lyme rash does not exclude the diagnosis. Approximately what proportion of patients with Lyme disease develop erythema migrans?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans appears in roughly 70 to 80 percent of patients with Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rash is present in about 70 to 80 percent of patients, meaning that a substantial minority never develop it. More than 30 percent of patients never get the classic bull's-eye appearance, and the rash may take many atypical forms or be absent entirely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the frequency of the hallmark rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is closer to the proportion who never develop the classic bull's-eye form, not the proportion with any rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This underestimates the frequency with which erythema migrans appears.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rash is not nearly universal; atypical presentations without rash are well recognized.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops several new annular rashes, shooting pains in his arms and legs, and a right-sided facial droop 6 weeks after a tick bite. An electrocardiogram shows heart block. Which structure is most commonly involved in the conduction abnormality at this stage of Lyme disease?

explanation.summary: Heart block in early disseminated Lyme disease usually involves the atrioventricular node.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stage 2, early disseminated Lyme disease, occurs within weeks to months of the bite and features multiple rashes, dispersed musculoskeletal pain, meningitis, facial (Bell) palsy, inflammation of the heart, and heart block that usually involves the atrioventricular node.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Block at the bundle of His is not the characteristic site of involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated left bundle branch block is not the typical conduction finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Purkinje network is not the usual site of Lyme carditis conduction block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sinoatrial node dysfunction is not the conduction abnormality described in disseminated Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has recurrent swollen, warm knee joints beginning 14 months after an untreated tick-borne illness acquired in Connecticut. Which of the following best characterizes the arthritis of late disseminated Lyme disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymmetric, intermittent large-joint involvement, especially the knees

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monoarticular great toe involvement with crystal deposition in fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent axial involvement with fusion of the sacroiliac joints

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symmetric proximal muscle weakness without any joint swelling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symmetric small-joint involvement of the hands with morning stiffness

explanation.summary: Lyme arthritis is asymmetric and intermittent, affects large joints such as the knees, and comes with swelling and warmth.
explanation.whyCorrect: During stage 3, which occurs months to years after the bite, most patients with arthritis have bouts of severe joint inflammation. The arthritis is distinguished from other forms in that it is associated with swelling and warmth, may be migratory, is intermittent, and is often asymmetric, with a predilection for large joints, especially the knees.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Crystal-associated monoarthritis of the great toe describes a different disease process entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Axial disease with sacroiliac fusion is not a feature of late Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late Lyme disease produces joint inflammation with swelling and warmth, not painless proximal muscle weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symmetric small-joint disease of the hands is not the pattern described for Lyme arthritis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man completed antibiotic therapy for Lyme disease 8 months ago, and there is no evidence of ongoing infection. He still reports muscle and joint pain, cognitive difficulty, disturbed sleep, and fatigue. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coinfection with Rickettsia rickettsii from the same bite

choices.label: B
choices.text: Persistent bacteremia from an inadequate antibiotic dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of latent spirochetes in the nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relapse of Lyme disease from antibiotic-resistant Borrelia burgdorferi

explanation.summary: Lingering symptoms after antibiotics have cleared Borrelia burgdorferi define post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients have lingering symptoms even after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection. Common complaints are muscle and joint pains, cognitive issues, sleep disturbance, and fatigue. The cause is unknown, though there is some evidence for an autoimmune response triggered by Borrelia burgdorferi. It is often colloquially called chronic Lyme disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A rickettsial coinfection would present as an acute febrile illness, not months of fatigue and cognitive complaints.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no ongoing bacteremia; the infection has been documented as cleared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactivation of latent spirochetes is not the described mechanism for persistent post-treatment symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The infection has been cleared; ongoing resistant infection is not the explanation for these symptoms.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of patients treated for Lyme disease continue to have lingering symptoms after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection?

explanation.summary: Roughly 10 to 20 percent of treated patients have persistent symptoms, a condition called post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 10 to 20 percent of patients will have lingering symptoms even after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection. This is post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, with muscle and joint pains, cognitive issues, sleep disturbance, and fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This markedly underestimates how common persistent post-treatment symptoms are.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is far lower than the reported frequency of persistent symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overestimates the proportion with lingering symptoms after treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Half of treated patients do not go on to have persistent symptoms.

questions.stem: Borrelia burgdorferi is a spirochete. Which of the following structures is responsible for its characteristic motility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polar flagellum anchored outside the outer membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoflagella, also called axial filaments, within the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gliding motility from surface adhesion protein complexes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peritrichous flagella distributed over the cell surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV pili that retract to pull the cell forward

explanation.summary: Spirochetes move using endoflagella (axial filaments), a structure internal to the cell envelope.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spirochetes have a complex cell wall resembling that of gram-negative bacteria, with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane, plus a unique structure called an endoflagella or axial filament that contributes to their motility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An externally anchored polar flagellum is not the spirochete arrangement; the flagella lie within the cell envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes do not rely on surface adhesion gliding for movement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritrichous external flagella are found in other bacteria, not in spirochetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV pilus-driven twitching motility is not the mechanism used by spirochetes.

questions.stem: A laboratory attempts to visualize Borrelia burgdorferi in a skin biopsy from a patient with suspected Lyme disease. Which of the following best describes this organism's cell wall and staining behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gram-negative envelope that is readily seen on routine Gram stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: A gram-negative-like envelope, but it stains poorly on Gram stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan layer that stains crisply as gram-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: An acid-fast envelope owing to mycolic acids in the cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: No cell wall at all, so that no stain will reveal the organism

explanation.summary: Spirochetes have a gram-negative-type envelope but stain poorly with Gram stain, so special stains are needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi has a complex cell wall similar to that of gram-negative bacteria, with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane. Despite this, spirochetes do not stain well by Gram stain, and special stains must be used for optimal visualization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although the envelope resembles that of gram-negative bacteria, the organism is not readily seen on routine Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The peptidoglycan layer is thin, not thick, and the organism is not gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acid-fastness from mycolic acids is a feature of a different group of organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spirochetes do have a cell wall; the problem is that it takes up Gram stain poorly.
